attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The draft keeps the amoral and misuse characterisation and the two-month remediation qualifier. 'Many harmful purposes' is a fair paraphrase of 'a whole range of nasty purposes'.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: safeguards still allowed several harmful uses in early February 2023. It treats 'amoral' as unreliable safeguards and asks about capability, not consistent success.

evidence.note: VICE, Feb 8, 2023: DAN role-play got ChatGPT to produce slurs and conspiracy theories, with new DAN versions on Feb 4 and Feb 7. It also mentions added filters by Feb 7.

CNBC's own test: DAN at first complied, including on violent content, then refused. Success was sporadic. This limits how reliable the jailbreak was but does not refute that misuse was possible. The URL is dated Feb 6; available_at says Feb 8.
OpenAI's own release notes show model updates on Jan 9 and Jan 30, before the February examples. They do not measure how intensive the safety remediation was.
Dark Reading, Feb 8, 2023: DAN bypassed restrictions on violent or illegal content, though not every time. It relies on CNBC, so it is not independent.

reviews.rationale: Reports from early February 2023 (VICE; Dark Reading via CNBC) document ChatGPT being jailbroken into slurs, conspiracy theories and violent content after the January updates. CNBC's refusals show the jailbreak was inconsistent, but under the contract refusals do not defeat a claim about what was possible. The fair reading of the claim is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The draft keeps the claim that RLHF is the only restraint and the claim about OpenAI's secrecy. Calling it causal fits, because it assigns RLHF the sole role in holding back worse output.

contract.note: 'The only thing' is the speaker's own exclusivity wording, so testing for other deployed safeguards is fair. The contract rightly refuses to count supervised fine-tuning as a separate safeguard. One tension: Marcus ties the Kenyan-labelled data to the same system.

evidence.note: TIME, Jan 18, 2023, quoting OpenAI: a toxicity detector built from Kenyan labelling was built into ChatGPT, and toxic data was filtered from training sets. Both are protections beyond RLHF. Their separate effects are not measured.

OpenAI's launch post (company disclosure) describes the RLHF pipeline only at a high level. The moderation safeguard it is cited for is not in the visible excerpt. Consistent with limited ChatGPT-specific disclosure.
The InstructGPT paper sets out the general RLHF method publicly. It is a predecessor model, so it does not settle ChatGPT-specific disclosure or causal effects.

reviews.rationale: The main causal claim is that RLHF was the only thing restraining ChatGPT. OpenAI's confirmation to TIME that a toxicity detector was built into ChatGPT, and that training data was filtered, meets the contract's contradiction condition. The secrecy part is not disproved: the disclosures are high-level. But the packet does not affirmatively establish it either, so the claim as a whole is contradicted.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The core claim, that apparent control of toxic output was an illusion, is kept. The Tay and Galactica asides are rightly treated as background.

contract.note: Reading 'illusion' as apparent safety failing under adversarial prompting fits Marcus's own concessions that refusals are frequent. It is a fair, ordinary reading and does not require that the safeguards achieved nothing.

evidence.note: Dark Reading, Feb 8, 2023: the DAN prompt bypassed ChatGPT's restrictions on violent and illegal content, though not every time. It is second-hand via CNBC, which the contract allows.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from early February 2023 documents prompt-based bypasses of ChatGPT's toxic-content restrictions, which meets the support condition under the fair reading. The report admits the bypasses were not always successful, which fits Marcus's concession about frequent refusals. Nothing in the packet shows robust safety under adversarial testing.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Those data' refers back to the training data behind RLHF, including what the Kenyan workers labelled. Reading it as ChatGPT's RLHF and safety-training data is reasonable. The contract covers both possible referents.

contract.note: Testing whether the actual examples and labels were public is the ordinary meaning of 'open about data'. The rule that later reports count only if they explicitly cover the earlier status is strict but workable.

evidence.note: Science News Explores, Feb 16, 2023: OpenAI 'has not released' its code or training data. That phrasing covers every date up to Feb 16, so it necessarily covers Feb 11. 'Training data' in the broad sense includes the feedback and safety data.

reviews.rationale: A report five days after the post says OpenAI had not released its training data. If nothing had been released by Feb 16, nothing had been released on Feb 11, so this meets the contract's exception for later reports. The packet shows no public release of ChatGPT feedback or safety data. The support rests on one journalistic statement, but nothing cuts against it.
